narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 52% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability tipped just above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was denied.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your third-year grades had the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Placing in the first decile that year is well below the average of roughly the fifth or sixth decile among students who were accepted, signaling to the model that your academic performance trended downward.

Your family income worked in the opposite direction. Being in the high-income bracket pulled the prediction modestly toward success, since very few accepted students come from that background and the model has learned it correlates with slightly better outcomes.

Your LSAT score of 30 was the third most important factor. This score sits noticeably below the 37-point average of accepted students and therefore nudged the prediction toward failure, though less dramatically than your third-year grades.

Taken together, the model concluded your academic trajectory, especially the sharp drop in third-year performance, outweighed the positive signal from your family background.

You should focus on strengthening your academic record and consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score. Improving either of those areas would likely change the prediction in your favor for future applications. (218 words)
